reference.source: ATS/ERS classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias / Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A smoking-related interstitial lung disease occurring predominantly in current or former smokers in their fourth and fifth decades
Presents with insidious dry cough and exertional breathlessness, and finger clubbing may be present
The name is a historical misnomer: the alveolar spaces are filled with pigmented macrophages, not desquamated epithelial cells
High-resolution CT typically shows extensive, predominantly lower-zone and peripheral ground-glass opacity, sometimes with small cysts and limited reticulation
It lies on a spectrum with respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, which shows more centrilobular nodularity
Histology shows diffuse, uniform accumulation of macrophages within alveoli with relatively mild and even interstitial inflammation
Smoking cessation is the cornerstone of treatment and can produce substantial improvement
Corticosteroids are often added for persistent or progressive disease after stopping smoking
reference.pathophysiology: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia is a diffuse parenchymal lung disease closely linked to cigarette smoking. Inhaled smoke recruits large numbers of macrophages, which accumulate uniformly within the alveolar spaces and contain a fine golden-brown smoker's pigment. The interstitium shows mild, even thickening with a modest chronic inflammatory infiltrate and generally little fibrosis compared with usual interstitial pneumonia. The macrophage filling impairs gas exchange, producing ground-glass change on imaging and a restrictive defect with reduced diffusing capacity. Removal of the inciting exposure through smoking cessation often allows regression, distinguishing its behaviour from the progressive fibrosing pneumonias.
additionalDifferentials: Usual interstitial pneumonia / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT showing widespread lower-zone and peripheral ground-glass opacity
Detailed smoking history as both a diagnostic clue and the key therapeutic target
Pulmonary function tests demonstrating restriction with reduced diffusing capacity
Bronchoalveolar lavage showing pigmented smoker's macrophages
Surgical lung biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain, showing uniform intra-alveolar macrophage accumulation
Connective tissue disease serology and exposure history to exclude mimics
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness or hypoxaemia despite smoking cessation
Development of fibrosis or honeycombing on follow-up imaging
Failure to respond to smoking cessation and corticosteroids
Features suggesting an alternative fibrosing interstitial pneumonia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, particularly when patients stop smoking, and many stabilise or improve; a minority progress to fibrosis and respiratory impairment despite treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to make smoking cessation the primary intervention
Confusing the ground-glass pattern with an infective or fibrotic process
Being misled by the outdated 'desquamative' name into expecting epithelial shedding rather than macrophage filling
Overlooking the overlap with respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease
